@graph.name: Gun Control: Baby Boomers Have Lost Their Way
@graph.articleBody:
I'm a Baby Boomer. In the 60's and 70's we changed the world. If something didn't look right, we tried to make it right. We protested, we marched, we made noise, and we made people take notice. Some of us went to jail, some of us lost our lives. But we held strongly to our beliefs. We believed in peace and love, not war and hate. And we made a difference.

Where are we today? We run businesses, we take an active role on our communities, we run local and national politics, we are in leadership roles. But have we become the very people we protested against in the 60s? Have we forgotten how to fight for what is right? Have we lost our way?

When students were gunned down at Kent State, we protested even louder. Eventually, we made those in charge listen to us, and make changes. But what are we doing today? Our children are being gunned down in our schools....IN OUR SCHOOLS! And what are we doing about it? Where is our unified voice to shout out about what is right? We have arrived at that place to make the changes that are right for everyone, and yet we do nothing. We hide.

How have we become so complacent as to let guns kill our children and our grandchildren in the place they go to receive an education? Back in our school days, we had school drills to hide under our desk when we thought we might be attacked by foreign enemies. We built bomb shelters to survive against a nuclear attack. Did we ever think our children would have to practice drills to protect them from our own citizens? Could we ever imagine someone roaming the halls with an assault weapon seeing how many they can kill as quickly as they can before getting caught? We have found the enemy, and it is us.

It's time for the Baby Boomers to stand up again. To do what is right to protect not just ourselves now, but our children. It's time for us to find our way, again. Otherwise, all of the protests and noise we made in the 60's was for nothing. Let's do the right thing and protect our children, and embrace the peace and love that was our hallmark in the 60's. It's time to act.

@graph.name: Healthcare Magic: Now You See It; Now You Don't!
@graph.articleBody:
The new healthcare plan the Republicans are attempting to rush through Congress ran into a significant roadblock when the CBO indicated that over time about 24 million Americans would be without a healthcare plan. But wait! I thought Donald Trump said he would create a healthcare plan for every American. So, I guess this magic trick is one of a disappearing act. In fact, a more appropriate phrase would be: Now you have it; now you don't.

Obama took office in 2009 and wanted to address the fact that over 35 million Americans were without healthcare insurance. So he put a plan in place to address this concern. This plan was essentially a modified version of a Republican plan by Mitt Romney (RomneyCare). So, President Obama created the ACA which quickly became known as ObamaCare. This plan to help get healthcare insurance to the 35 million uninsured Americans met with tremendous resistance from Republicans. In the end, a very watered-down version of Obama's plan was "driven" through the Senate, much to the dismay of Republicans who felt the plan was "shoved down their throat."

Was it a perfect plan? No. But neither was Medicare and Medicaid when they were first introduced in 1964. It took years of tweaking to improve Medicare and Medicaid to where they are today. I don't believe anyone would argue with the fact that ObamaCare needs improving fast. But tearing it down and putting in place a plan that moves us in the opposite direction can never be mistaken for progress. Twenty million Americans became insured under ObamaCare, and the CBO now projects 24 million will become uninsured under the new replacement plan. So why are the Republicans pushing this plan through so quickly? They fought ObamaCare for so long and hard, and Trump promised to make it better for everyone, that they feel they need to do something quickly to comply with the President's directive to overhaul ObamaCare. But don't you think we should get it right, rather than get it done fast?

Leaving 24 million Americans without healthcare insurance, especially some of the most vulnerable aging population, is another example of a dysfunctional political system trying to fix a marketplace problem. What is really important is that we address the very issue of providing as many Americans as possible with affordable health insurance in a bipartisan approach that puts aside political wounds and party agendas for the good of the nation. Let's not make our health a political ping-pong ball.

@graph.name: Why Republicans Can't Fix ACA?
@graph.articleBody:
The reason Republicans cannot fix ACA, or Obamacare, is because it is not a political issue, it is a business issue. Let's wind the clock back a bit to see where the problem is today.

Before the ACA was passed, there were about 38 million Americans uninsured, and many more under-insured. Taking a page out of the Romney healthcare playbook, the Obama Administration adopted the idea of insuring everyone through exchanges. Many insurance companies lined-up to be on these exchanges in order to offer health insurance to these uninsured, especially since the government was going to help pay for it. But the insurance companies had to bid blindly for the rates they would charge for their plans. So in order to ensure they got their share of these uninsured Americans, many insurance companies bid a bit too low (despite having an army of actuaries that would calculate in infamous "medical-loss ratio").

Then the unexpected happened (actually, most people could have predicted this). All these people who had gone for a long time without medical insurance flooded into the healthcare system. And many had serious illnesses that had been waiting to get treated for some time. The health costs to these insurance companies exceeded their expectations, and they began to "lose" money on these patients. So many of the "big players" pulled out of the exchanges, leaving smaller players to insure these high-cost patients. Now, it's not too hard to figure out what these remaining insurers had to do to stay in business. You guessed it, "raise their premiums."

Soon, the Affordable Care Act became the Unaffordable Care Act. Imagine 20 million Americans pouring into the healthcare system for the first time in probably a long time. It seemed overwhelming to these insurance providers. Now think "lag time." The flood of newly insured patients receiving treatments for pent-up aliments would appear overwhelming at first, but over time, things would stabilize. But insurance companies that lose money one year need to raise rate the second year to cover their losses, or eventually they are out of business. Costs didn't come down as fast as some insurers thought, so up go the rates again. Eventually, the insurers would find the right balance between in-coming revenues and out-going payments, if they hung in there long enough.

So, how do Republicans fix this problem? Well, they could do nothing and over time the problem would likely fix itself. Maybe. If enough young healthy people buy insurance plans, the blending of healthy and unhealthy patients would balance itself out. Maybe. We have the Baby-Boomers aging out fast, so there may not be enough healthy young people to cover for all the unhealthy Baby-Boomers. We could force the big insurance companies to get back into these exchanges and lower their premiums, and potentially lose money. That is certainly one "strong-arm" approach the Republicans could take, and under their leadership of Trump, this could certainly be an option they might consider. But the business issue is one of pooling enough healthy people with unhealthy ones to be able to offer an insurance plan with reasonable rates for all. Business issues usually fix themselves because competition has a way of following Darwin's principle of "the survival of the strongest."

There is one last possible solution to fixing healthcare delivery in America. That is the unspeakable "Universal Healthcare." In most countries in the world with healthcare delivery (like more than 99%), there is a single payer, the government. If there were no insurance companies competing for private and public business in the United States, and everyone was blended or pooled across the nation under a single payer system (i.e. universal healthcare), then we wouldn't need these exchanges forcing insurance companies to cover some very unhealthy people, we wouldn't have insurance companies "cherry-picking" the healthiest people to insure, we wouldn't need to worry about the dreaded "medical-loss ratio," and a lot of employers could get back to the business they are in instead of being in the healthcare business by having to offer insurance to their employees.

Will the Republicans consider a universal healthcare system? I seriously doubt it. If the Democrats couldn't implement anything that resembled a single payer system, it is unlikely the business-favoring Republicans would implement such a plan. So, that is why I do not believe the Republicans will really fix ACA, other than to maybe change the name and polish it up a bit. But I don't think Trumpcare has the same ring to it!
